### HTTP proxies (2) 

browser$\rightarrow$HTTP(S) proxy sever: <br> 
```
GET http://example.com/somesite HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
...

```
<hr/>

* instead of path, can put full URL
* doesn't have to be <code>http</code> URL


### proxy functionality  {.smaller}


* caching for multiple users 

   * reason for <code>Cache-Control: private</code>

* filtering content 

   * antimalware, adblocking, etc.

* logging content (example: debugging webapp)
* …


###  

![](/http/texfig/proxies_2.figure.svg){fig-alt="user-agent sends request specifying which web server to contact to forward proxy server, which sends normal request to web server. user-agent sends _normal_ request to a reverse proxy server, which sends a request to a backend server, chosen based on the user-agent request path."}


### reverse proxy  {.smaller}


* why not just go directly to actual web server? 
<hr class="vspace" />
* make multiple web severs appear as one? example: 

   * https://example.com/foo/XXX goes to https://foo-backend.example.com/XXX
   * https://example.com/bar/XXX goes to https://bar-backend.example.com/XXX
   * https://example.com/ goes to https://frontpage.example.com/

* do caching, filtering, or similar on behalf of webservers
* split requests between multiple identical servers for performance


### non-HTTP in HTTP proxy  {.smaller}

[]{.my-small} client $\rightarrow$ server: 
```
CONNECT ns.foo.com:53 HTTP/1.1
Host: ns.foo.com:50

```
<hr/>
server $\rightarrow$ client: 
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Some-header: some-value


```
<hr>
client $\rightarrow$ server: (dns request) <br> server $\rightarrow$ client: (dns response from ns.foo.com) <br> client $\rightarrow$ server: (dns request) <br> server $\rightarrow$ client: (dns response from ns.foo.com) <br> …

### CONNECT 


* allows ‘‘tunnelling’’ arbitrary TCP connections through HTTP
* often not implemented by HTTP proxies and/or very restricted
